extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, storytellers, and students studying East Asian narrative forms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for structuring short narratives using the four-act Kishōtenketsu form (ki–shō–ten–ketsu), explaining the role of each act, distinguishing features versus Western three-act structures, and explicit evaluation criteria for the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ki (起 — Introduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishes characters, setting, era, and context. Introduces the world without conflict. Translates as 'rouse' or 'wake up.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should set up the world and situational baseline rather than a problem to be solved; avoid introducing major conflict here. Use this act to orient readers to characters and milieu so later acts can reframe them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shō (承 — Development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expands and develops what was introduced. No major changes; deepens situation and character. Sets up what the twist will pivot against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deepen detail and texture of the initial situation rather than escalate plot; prepare expectations and anchors that the ten will recontextualize. Avoid significant turning events or climactic escalation in this act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten (転 — Twist / Turn)
rubrics_metrics.description: The crux. An unexpected development reframes everything. Often introduces an apparently unrelated element that recontextualizes the prior acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The twist should genuinely reframe prior material (not merely escalate it). It is deliberately asymmetric in placement — major story content is often held back until this third act — so the ten can feel surprising and transformative. Anti-pattern: making the ten into just a midpoint escalation that fits Western three-act expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ketsu (結 — Conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolution; brings the disparate elements together to produce meaning. Translates as 'result, consequence, outcome.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ketsu should synthesize the juxtaposed elements established earlier to produce meaning rather than simply resolving a conflict. Expect a unifying or interpretive closure that ties the introduced and juxtaposed elements together.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement of conflict-centeredness
rubrics_metrics.description: No requirement of conflict as the engine of plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories may be driven by juxtaposition, mood, or observation rather than by antagonistic conflict. This allows forms like slice-of-life or contemplative narratives that would seem 'plotless' under Western conflict-centered criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric placement of turning point
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymmetric placement — the turning point is in the third of four acts (ten), not the middle of a three-act structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating structure, note that the expectation of a mid-story crisis (act 2 of 3) does not apply; the major transformative moment deliberately appears later. Scoring should reflect adherence to this placement rather than forcing Western pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition over causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The twist often shifts the meaning of prior acts rather than escalating them; the structure favors juxtaposition over causal escalation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value how well two seemingly disparate elements are placed side-by-side to produce new meaning; do not penalize lack of causal linkage if juxtaposition yields resonance. Anti-pattern: forcing causal linkage where the form expects contrast or reframing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for slice-of-life and contemplative narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Allows for slice-of-life and contemplative narratives that would seem 'plotless' by Western criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should recognize quality in mood, observation, or thematic resonance rather than only plotting or conflict resolution. Examples include quiet character studies or descriptive pieces that culminate in an interpretive ketsu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether each act fulfills its structural role
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should consider whether each act (ki, shō, ten, ketsu) fulfills its structural role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the introduction orients, the development deepens without major change, the turn reframes, and the conclusion synthesizes. Deduct where acts are blurred or fail to perform their expected function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the ten genuinely reframes (not merely escalates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the ten genuinely reframes earlier material rather than only escalating plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for an unexpected element that recontextualizes prior acts. If the ten functions merely as escalation or a conventional midpoint twist, it fails this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the ketsu synthesizes rather than resolves a conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the ketsu synthesizes juxtaposed elements to produce meaning, rather than simply resolving a conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ketsu should integrate the introduced and turned elements into a coherent outcome or insight. If the conclusion only ties up conflict without synthesis, it may be inconsistent with Kishōtenketsu practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence between juxtaposed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Coherence between juxtaposed elements (how well the disparate pieces relate once the ten reframes them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how convincingly the ketsu connects or harmonizes the previously juxtaposed elements. Weak or arbitrary links are an anti-pattern; strong resonance or emergent meaning is a positive sign.
